public_rationale: In 2025 the US institute was renamed CAISI. It kept a focus on guidance, testing and evaluation under a light-touch approach (e1), and it works through voluntary agreements with developers (e2). An explainer on both the US and UK institutes says neither has legal authority to block a model's release, because their testing agreements are voluntary (e3). A 2025 UK petition asking that the UK institute be given power to block threatening models shows it lacked that power (e4). The institutes offered guidance but had little legal power to stop dangerous models, as forecast.
limitations: Covers only the US and UK institutes.
Key legal-authority statement comes from a secondary 2026 explainer describing the post-2025 position.

statement.excerpt: AI Safety Institutes will also offer guidance, but have little legal authority to stop truly dangerous models should they arise.
statement.document_title: 25 AI Predictions for 2025, from Marcus on AI

from_speaker: where we will be at the end of this year
our_interpretation: Plain reading: during 2025, the main national AI safety institutes (the US and UK institutes, including under their new names CAISI and the AI Security Institute) would issue guidance and run evaluations, but would lack legal power to block or halt a model's release.
'Should they arise' describes the hypothetical scope of the authority. It is not a condition on the forecast, so the claim is scored whether or not a dangerous model appeared.
Being renamed does not take the bodies out of scope.
criteria.support_condition: During 2025 the institutes work mainly through guidance, testing and voluntary agreements, and no statute gives them power to block a model's release.
criteria.contradiction_condition: During 2025 a major AI safety institute gains binding legal power to stop deployment of dangerous models, or stops offering guidance.
